stories.title: Suspected Drone Strike on Russian Ship in Benghazi Raises Security Concerns
stories.summary: A Russian warship, the Merkury, was reportedly struck by a suspected Ukrainian drone while docked at the naval base in Benghazi, Libya. The explosion caused significant damage to the vessel and ignited a fire at the facility. Local officials indicated that the ship was in Libya for fuel and supplies on its return journey to Russia. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, which raises concerns about the implications for regional security amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict.

timeline_highlights.title: Trump Issues Threats Against Iranian Infrastructure Amid Strait of Hormuz Tensions
timeline_highlights.summary: US President Donald Trump has threatened to target Iranian bridges and power plants in retaliation for any attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. He stated that for each ship fired upon by Iranian forces, the US would respond by destroying a corresponding piece of Iranian infrastructure. This escalation comes amid ongoing tensions in the region and rising oil prices.
key_facts: Trump threatened to destroy Iranian infrastructure for each ship attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The threat follows continued Iranian attacks on shipping in the region.
Oil prices have surged amid the escalating tensions.

timeline_highlights.title: Russian Strike on Kyiv Results in Eight Deaths and Extensive Damage
timeline_highlights.summary: A Russian attack on Kyiv on November 20, 2026, resulted in the deaths of at least eight people and left many injured. The assault was described by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as one of the largest of the war. Emergency crews are currently searching through the wreckage, battling fires, and assessing damage to buildings and warehouses across the capital.

timeline_highlights.title: Russian Strike on Apartment Building Near Kyiv Leaves Casualties and Trapped Residents
timeline_highlights.summary: A Russian strike on an apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, resulted in at least two confirmed deaths and several injuries. Nine individuals, including a child, were evacuated, while up to seven others are feared trapped under the rubble. Rescue operations are ongoing as authorities search for survivors in the collapsed structure.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

explore_lenses.label: Why does a strike in Benghazi matter?
explore_lenses.title: It could widen risks beyond the war zone
explore_lenses.summary: The reported damage is significant not only for Russia but also for Libya, where rival authorities fear that ports and civilian infrastructure could become venues for outside powers' conflict. The available evidence confirms a major incident at the port, but not who caused it.

claims.text: Satellite imagery published by AP showed the Russian corvette Merkury capsized at Benghazi naval base after the reported incident; Libyan military officials said the ship was severely damaged and a fire was ignited at the facility.

Libya's Tripoli-based government said it rejects turning Libyan ports and civilian facilities into an arena for external powers to settle conflicts, framing the event as a threat to Libyan sovereignty and public safety rather than a Libyan role in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The U.N. Panel of Experts has documented continuing scrutiny of foreign military transport and naval activity in Libya under the arms-embargo framework, underscoring why the presence and use of military vessels in Libyan ports carry broader security and legal consequences.

story_report.summary: A Russian corvette, the Merkury, was damaged in an apparent drone strike while docked at Libya’s Benghazi naval base, triggering a fire at the facility. Satellite imagery published by AP showed the vessel capsized after the incident. Eastern Libyan authorities said the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies while returning to Russia, while no group has claimed responsibility and the reported Ukrainian connection remains unverified.

sections.heading: Drone Attribution Remains Unverified
sections.body: Unnamed Libyan military officials alleged that two sea drones launched from a base used by Ukrainian forces in western Libya struck the corvette. The officials are affiliated with the Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv had publicly commented in the reporting reviewed, and no public forensic evidence independently established a Ukrainian launch site, the weapon used, or those responsible.

sections.heading: Libyan Authorities Raise Sovereignty Concerns
sections.body: Libya’s Tripoli-based government said it rejected the use of Libyan ports and civilian facilities as an arena for external powers to settle conflicts, describing the incident as a threat to sovereignty and public safety. The eastern administration likewise called it an infringement on sovereignty and maritime safety, saying port operations could resume once the fire was controlled and the site secured. Libya remains divided between the U.N.-supported Tripoli government and a rival eastern administration.

sections.heading: Foreign Military Activity Faces Scrutiny
sections.body: The U.N. Panel of Experts has continued to scrutinize foreign military transport and naval activity in Libya under the arms-embargo framework. The panel said Russia’s information about military flights to Libya was insufficient for its compliance review, limiting public visibility into some foreign military logistics. The eastern government said the Merkury’s stop was covered by maritime-cooperation arrangements with Russia, but did not publicly detail its cargo.

unresolved.text: It remains unclear whether investigators will publish technical findings, publicly attribute the incident, or independently assess damage and injuries.

Dashcam footage captured the blast as a car reversed away from the scene. Regional authorities and police said Russian forces attacked the wider Lviv region overnight and into the morning with missiles and drones, while air defenses operated for nearly six hours.

sections.heading: Lviv Transport and Power Damage
sections.body: Regional authorities said Sknyliv station had the most casualties and that its ticket offices were damaged. Police also reported damage to an energy-infrastructure facility in Stryi district, prompting emergency and scheduled power-outage regimes across the Lviv region. Security Service investigators in the Lviv region, supervised by the regional prosecutor’s office, opened a pretrial investigation under Article 438 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code concerning war crimes. Zelenskyy said restoration work was under way where security conditions allowed and urged partners to speed delivery of air-defense systems and interceptor missiles.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

explore_lenses.label: Why did air defenses not prevent the Dymer strike?
explore_lenses.title: A large drone barrage still produced multiple impacts
explore_lenses.summary: The Dymer building was hit during a nationwide overnight drone attack, not as an isolated incident. Ukraine reported substantial interceptions, but also confirmed strikes across numerous locations.

claims.text: Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 186 attack and decoy drones from the evening of November 21 through the morning of November 22; it said 161 were downed or suppressed by 08:00, while impacts were recorded at 18 locations.
Euronews reported that the Dymer strike destroyed a section of the five-storey residential building from the first through fifth floors and was part of the wider overnight drone wave.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy argued that delays in supplying anti-ballistic interceptors were difficult to justify and urged partners to authorize transfers already funded through NATO's PURL initiative.

explore_lenses.label: Why are the casualty and missing counts changing?
explore_lenses.title: Rescuers' counts are evolving as rubble is cleared
explore_lenses.summary: Initial reports described up to seven people potentially trapped, while later official statements cited 14 people unaccounted for. These figures reflect different stages and categories of an active search, rather than a settled final toll.

claims.text: Ukraine's State Emergency Service initially said up to seven people could be trapped, while Zelenskyy later said 14 people were unaccounted for; nine residents, including a child, had been evacuated.

The Associated Press reported later on November 22 that the morning strike had destroyed the Dymer building, killed three people and buried others, indicating that the confirmed fatality count had changed as the operation continued.
The discrepancy between people described as trapped, missing, evacuated, injured, and confirmed dead means the available figures should not be combined into a single casualty total.

story_report.summary: A Russian strike destroyed part of a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, prompting a search for residents believed to be beneath the rubble. Initial reports recorded at least two deaths and four injuries, while nine people, including a child, were evacuated. Later reporting by the Associated Press put the death toll at three, as rescue work continued. Authorities have issued differing figures for people unaccounted for, with up to seven initially feared trapped and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later saying 14 people were missing.

sections.heading: Overnight Drone Attack Across Ukraine
sections.body: Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 186 attack and decoy drones from the evening of November 21 through the morning of November 22. By 08:00, it said 161 had been downed or suppressed, while impacts were recorded at 18 locations. Euronews described the Dymer strike as part of the wider overnight drone wave. Zelenskyy said delays in providing anti-ballistic interceptors were difficult to justify and urged partners to approve transfers funded through NATO’s PURL initiative.

sections.heading: Rescue Teams Search Collapsed Building
sections.body: Emergency workers used ladders and an aerial platform to evacuate residents from the damaged structure, while rescuers continued searching the debris for survivors. Kyiv regional authorities set up a command center at the site, where social services and psychologists were coordinating assistance. The reported death, injury and missing-person figures may change as teams reach and identify people in the collapsed sections.

unresolved.text: Authorities had not published a final accounting of residents, survivors or deaths, and the reported categories of trapped, missing, evacuated, injured and dead should not be combined into a single casualty total.

The available reporting does not establish which flight path or specific air-defence failure led to the Dymer impact; the Air Force’s morning figures were preliminary and some drones were reportedly still airborne.

The operation involved cooperation with US intelligence and included a shootout between security forces and armed members of his cartel.

event_overview.title: About Mexican Drug Cartels
event_overview.subject: Mexican Drug Cartels
event_overview.summary: The event concerns the Mexican military’s November 2026 capture of Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” following a U.S.-supported investigation, and the violence reported in Sinaloa during and after the operation. Meza-Flores had long been identified by U.S. authorities as an alleged senior figure in Sinaloa-based drug-trafficking networks and faced U.S. federal criminal charges.

facts.label: Capture
facts.value: The U.S. Department of Justice said Meza-Flores was captured by the Mexican military on November 20-21, 2026, after a Homeland Security Task Force investigation; Mexican forces carried out the arrest.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: The operation and ensuing unrest were centered in Sinaloa, a northwestern Mexican state; the Meza-Flores organization was previously described by the U.S. Treasury as operating from Guasave, Sinaloa.

facts.label: Identity and organization
facts.value: U.S. authorities identify Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores by the aliases “El Chapo Isidro,” “Chapo Isidro,” and “Chapito Isidro.” A 2019 Justice Department announcement described him as the alleged leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, a major trafficking organization based in Sinaloa.

facts.label: U.S. criminal case
facts.value: A federal superseding indictment alleged that, from about January 2005 through November 2019, Meza-Flores conspired to distribute cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, and marijuana for importation into the United States, and alleged firearms offenses. These were charges, not findings of guilt.

facts.label: Cartel classification in U.S. policy
facts.value: The Justice Department states that the U.S. Secretary of State designated the Sinaloa Cartel as a Foreign Terrorist Organization and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist on February 20, 2025; this is a U.S. legal designation and does not itself determine individual criminal liability.

event_overview.scope_note: This timeline covers the November 2026 capture and immediate violence in Sinaloa, not the full history of the Sinaloa Cartel, the Beltrán Leyva network, or every related prosecution and security operation.

claims.text: The FBI records that Meza-Flores was added to its Ten Most Wanted list on February 4, 2025 and removed after Mexican authorities arrested him in Guasave on November 20, 2026.

A U.S. Justice Department release says a District of Columbia indictment charges him with, among other offenses, leading a continuing criminal enterprise, drug-importation conspiracy, money laundering, firearms offenses, material support for a terrorist organization, and narcoterrorism; these are allegations, not convictions.

U.S. prosecutors say the investigation was conducted through a Homeland Security Task Force, while Mexican reporting citing the Defense Ministry says the operation used bilateral intelligence coordination.

story_report.summary: Mexican military forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Nov. 20, triggering a violent response that killed at least 11 people. The FBI had listed him among its Ten Most Wanted fugitives since February 2025. Mexican authorities reported a raid and shootout, followed by armed attacks, roadblocks and burned freight vehicles as security forces moved to contain the unrest.

sections.heading: U.S. Case Against Meza-Flores
sections.body: A U.S. indictment accuses Meza-Flores of leading a continuing criminal enterprise and of drug-importation conspiracy, money laundering, firearms offenses, material support for a terrorist organization and narcoterrorism. Those are allegations rather than convictions. The Justice Department said that, if convicted in the U.S. case, he could face the death penalty or mandatory life imprisonment; prosecutors said their investigation was conducted through a Homeland Security Task Force.

sections.heading: Guasave Operation Leaves Eleven Dead
sections.body: Mexico’s Defense Ministry said seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed in the operation. State authorities said an interinstitutional security response, backed by Black Hawk helicopters and surveillance drones, was under way after attacks on federal personnel, roadblocks and vehicle fires. U.S. prosecutors allege Meza-Flores commanded gunmen across areas including Guasave, Los Mochis and remote parts of Sinaloa; AP reported he was allied with the Los Mayos faction in a wider struggle for control of the state.

sections.heading: Security Presence and Custody Questions
sections.body: Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch said armed forces would remain in Sinaloa to protect civilians and described the detention as an important step toward pacifying the state. Whether the arrest produces a sustained reduction in violence remains uncertain, as criminal organizations can retain personnel, territory and financial operations after a leader’s detention.

unresolved.text: Authorities have not publicly detailed the intelligence-sharing and operational roles behind the arrest, despite accounts of bilateral intelligence coordination.
It remains unclear whether every reported shooting, fire and blockade was centrally directed by Meza-Flores’s organization or involved separate armed groups acting independently.

explore_lenses.label: Why are fatal boat accidents recurring in Nigeria?
explore_lenses.title: Safety rules exist, but enforcement gaps persist
explore_lenses.summary: This disaster fits a wider inland-waterway safety problem rather than an isolated event. Official and policy sources identify preventable operating risks alongside weather and waterway hazards.

claims.text: NIWA’s public incident dataset records 22 inland-waterway mishaps in 2025 involving 672 people, with 237 listed casualties; it includes two Bayelsa incidents before this latest capsize.
NEMA identifies overloading, night travel, poor maintenance, untrained operators, limited life-jacket use and weak enforcement as recurring contributors to boat mishaps.

A National Institute for Legislative and Democratic Studies issue brief argues that gaps in inspections, monitoring, funding and inter-agency coordination allow unsafe practices to continue despite NIWA’s regulatory mandate.

story_report.summary: At least 24 people died after a boat carrying mourners to a funeral capsized in southern Nigeria’s Bayelsa State. Emergency teams recovered 24 bodies while search-and-rescue operations continued, and police said another 24 people had been rescued and given medical assistance. President Bola Tinubu directed federal disaster-response agencies to coordinate recovery and rescue efforts and offered condolences to the victims’ families and Bayelsa authorities.

sections.heading: Police Examine Boat Mechanical Problem

Passengers reportedly asked the operator to steer toward land, but the operator allegedly fled, while the boat manager was taken into custody. The Bayelsa State government said overloading, speeding, recklessness and travelling without life jackets must stop, characterising compliance by both operators and passengers as central to preventing further accidents.

sections.heading: Inland Waterway Safety Record
sections.body: Nigeria’s Inland Waterways Authority recorded 22 inland-waterway mishaps involving 672 people in 2025, with 237 casualties listed in its public incident dataset; the record includes two Bayelsa incidents preceding the latest capsize. NEMA has identified overloading, night travel, poor maintenance, untrained operators, limited life-jacket use and weak enforcement as recurring contributors to boat mishaps. A legislative institute brief has also cited shortcomings in inspections, monitoring, funding and coordination among agencies.

sections.heading: Waterway Rules and Safety Equipment
sections.body: Nigeria’s accident-investigation body has documented that inland-waterway vessels are expected to have qualified boatmasters and life-saving equipment, including life jackets, buoys, rafts and fire extinguishers. NIWA says its regulatory responsibilities include vessel registration and licensing, navigation protocols and enforcement. Any sanctions or broader safety measures will depend on the results of the continuing response and investigation.

Investigators had not established whether mechanical failure, overcrowding, absent safety equipment, navigation decisions or another factor caused the sinking, and no official investigative report or charging decision was publicly available.

stories.title: Fire at Indonesian Confectionery Factory Leaves Three Dead and Dozens Missing
stories.summary: A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta, Indonesia, has resulted in at least three fatalities, with 36 individuals reported missing. The blaze, which began in a cooling unit on the third floor, has left parts of the factory severely damaged, including a collapsed roof. Firefighters continue to battle the flames more than 12 hours after the incident started, while rescue efforts are underway to locate the missing persons.

event_overview.title: About West Bank Violence
event_overview.subject: West Bank Violence
event_overview.summary: West Bank violence refers to recurring attacks, confrontations and other coercive incidents affecting Palestinians, Israeli settlers and Israeli forces across the West Bank, including damage to people, homes, farmland, livestock and essential infrastructure. The November 2026 developments concern alleged settler attacks on Palestinian communities within a wider pattern that UN humanitarian monitors document separately from other forms of violence in the territory.

facts.label: Location and context
facts.value: The West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is treated by the United Nations and the International Court of Justice as part of the Occupied Palestinian Territory; the ICJ’s July 19, 2024 advisory opinion addressed Israeli policies and practices there, including settlements and settler violence.

facts.label: Legal framework
facts.value: UN Security Council Resolution 2334, adopted in 2016, states that Israeli settlements in Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, have no legal validity under international law. Israel disputes this characterization and maintains claims and security positions concerning the territory.

facts.label: How incidents are tracked
facts.value: OCHA has documented West Bank casualties since 2005 and settler violence since 2006, counting settler attacks that result in Palestinian casualties, property damage, or both.

facts.label: Recent pattern
facts.value: OCHA recorded more than 1,600 settler attacks causing Palestinian casualties and/or property damage from January through mid-September 2026, affecting 275 Palestinian communities; reported effects included injuries, arson and damage to homes, crops, water systems and other infrastructure.

facts.label: Displacement impact
facts.value: OCHA reported that settler attacks and related access restrictions displaced more than 6,500 Palestinians between January 2023 and August 2026, alongside damage to livelihoods and essential services.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows the selected November 22, 2026 attacks and related Israeli political reaction; it does not attempt to catalogue all West Bank violence, settlement activity, military operations, legal claims or wider Israeli-Palestinian conflict developments.

event_overview.summary: This event concerns the 2026 election for North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District, a contest for one seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. The closely decided race drew attention because its outcome contributes to the partisan composition and control of the House for the next Congress.

facts.label: Election date
facts.value: North Carolina held its 2026 statewide general election on November 3, 2026; all 14 of the state’s U.S. House seats were on the ballot.

facts.label: Office and candidates
facts.value: The contest was for U.S. House District 5. The state candidate list identifies Democrat Charles Noble “Chuck” Hubbard, Republican Virginia Foxx, and Libertarian Robert B. Luffman as candidates.

facts.label: Election administration and recount rule
facts.value: The North Carolina State Board of Elections has jurisdiction over this nonstatewide congressional contest. State law permits a candidate to demand a recount when the margin is no more than 1% of votes cast; Foxx requested one after the county canvasses reported a 331-vote margin.

facts.label: Congressional term
facts.value: House members serve two-year terms; under the Twentieth Amendment, the terms of incoming representatives begin at noon on January 3, so the election determines representation for the Congress beginning in January 2027.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows the Hubbard–Foxx result and its relevance to the U.S. House majority, not every North Carolina race, statewide election issue, recount procedure, or subsequent action in Congress.

sections.heading: Recount Process in North Carolina

The State Board said machine recounts were expected to finish before its Nov. 24 meeting on statewide certification; its process also allows a candidate to seek a hand-to-eye recount using bipartisan teams and public observation safeguards.

sections.heading: Foxx Loss Expands Democratic Leeway

The larger House majority gives Democrats more room to pass party-line legislation in the chamber, though it does not determine Senate action or whether measures become law.

event_overview.summary: This event concerns the 2026 election for North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District, a contest for one seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. The closely decided race drew attention because its outcome contributes to the partisan composition and control of the House for the next Congress.

facts.label: Election date
facts.value: North Carolina held its 2026 statewide general election on November 3, 2026; all 14 of the state’s U.S. House seats were on the ballot.

facts.label: Office and candidates
facts.value: The contest was for U.S. House District 5. The state candidate list identifies Democrat Charles Noble “Chuck” Hubbard, Republican Virginia Foxx, and Libertarian Robert B. Luffman as candidates.

facts.label: Election administration and recount rule
facts.value: The North Carolina State Board of Elections has jurisdiction over this nonstatewide congressional contest. State law permits a candidate to demand a recount when the margin is no more than 1% of votes cast; Foxx requested one after the county canvasses reported a 331-vote margin.

facts.label: Congressional term
facts.value: House members serve two-year terms; under the Twentieth Amendment, the terms of incoming representatives begin at noon on January 3, so the election determines representation for the Congress beginning in January 2027.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows the Hubbard–Foxx result and its relevance to the U.S. House majority, not every North Carolina race, statewide election issue, recount procedure, or subsequent action in Congress.

event_overview.title: About Climate Change
event_overview.subject: Climate Change
event_overview.summary: COP31 was the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference, the annual negotiating session for parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It brought governments together in Antalya, Türkiye, alongside accredited observers and other stakeholders, to negotiate and advance international action on emissions reductions, adaptation and climate finance under the UN climate treaties.

facts.label: Dates and venue
facts.value: The conference was scheduled for 9-20 November 2026 at the Antalya EXPO Center in Soğucaksu, Antalya, Türkiye.

facts.label: Institutional basis
facts.value: COP31 was the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the 1992 UNFCCC, the framework treaty that underpins the international climate-negotiation process and is the parent treaty to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

facts.label: Meeting format
facts.value: The gathering also convened CMP21, the meeting of parties to the Kyoto Protocol, and CMA8, the meeting of parties to the Paris Agreement; these linked bodies consider matters under their respective treaties.

facts.label: Hosts and leadership
facts.value: Türkiye hosted the conference, with Murat Kurum nominated as COP31 President; Australia’s Chris Bowen served as President of Negotiations under the Türkiye-Australia partnership arrangements.

facts.label: Participants and access
facts.value: Parties to the UNFCCC sent leaders and negotiators, while accredited observer groups—including UN bodies, intergovernmental organizations, NGOs, business representatives, scientists, Indigenous Peoples and youth—could participate under UNFCCC procedures. Official negotiating meetings were held in the registered-participant Blue Zone; the host-managed Green Zone was intended for public-facing activities.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the conference’s opening and its reported collapse over fossil-fuel language; it does not attempt to catalogue every negotiation text, side event, national statement or issue discussed during COP31.

event_overview.title: About West Bank Violence
event_overview.subject: West Bank Violence
event_overview.summary: West Bank violence refers to recurring attacks, confrontations and other coercive incidents affecting Palestinians, Israeli settlers and Israeli forces across the West Bank, including damage to people, homes, farmland, livestock and essential infrastructure. The November 2026 developments concern alleged settler attacks on Palestinian communities within a wider pattern that UN humanitarian monitors document separately from other forms of violence in the territory.

facts.label: Location and context
facts.value: The West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is treated by the United Nations and the International Court of Justice as part of the Occupied Palestinian Territory; the ICJ’s July 19, 2024 advisory opinion addressed Israeli policies and practices there, including settlements and settler violence.

facts.label: Legal framework
facts.value: UN Security Council Resolution 2334, adopted in 2016, states that Israeli settlements in Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, have no legal validity under international law. Israel disputes this characterization and maintains claims and security positions concerning the territory.

facts.label: How incidents are tracked
facts.value: OCHA has documented West Bank casualties since 2005 and settler violence since 2006, counting settler attacks that result in Palestinian casualties, property damage, or both.

facts.label: Recent pattern
facts.value: OCHA recorded more than 1,600 settler attacks causing Palestinian casualties and/or property damage from January through mid-September 2026, affecting 275 Palestinian communities; reported effects included injuries, arson and damage to homes, crops, water systems and other infrastructure.

facts.label: Displacement impact
facts.value: OCHA reported that settler attacks and related access restrictions displaced more than 6,500 Palestinians between January 2023 and August 2026, alongside damage to livelihoods and essential services.

event_overview.title: About Climate Change
event_overview.subject: Climate Change
event_overview.summary: COP31 was the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference, the annual negotiating session for parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It brought governments together in Antalya, Türkiye, alongside accredited observers and other stakeholders, to negotiate and advance international action on emissions reductions, adaptation and climate finance under the UN climate treaties.

facts.label: Dates and venue
facts.value: The conference was scheduled for 9-20 November 2026 at the Antalya EXPO Center in Soğucaksu, Antalya, Türkiye.

facts.label: Institutional basis
facts.value: COP31 was the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the 1992 UNFCCC, the framework treaty that underpins the international climate-negotiation process and is the parent treaty to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

facts.label: Meeting format
facts.value: The gathering also convened CMP21, the meeting of parties to the Kyoto Protocol, and CMA8, the meeting of parties to the Paris Agreement; these linked bodies consider matters under their respective treaties.

facts.label: Hosts and leadership
facts.value: Türkiye hosted the conference, with Murat Kurum nominated as COP31 President; Australia’s Chris Bowen served as President of Negotiations under the Türkiye-Australia partnership arrangements.

facts.label: Participants and access
facts.value: Parties to the UNFCCC sent leaders and negotiators, while accredited observer groups—including UN bodies, intergovernmental organizations, NGOs, business representatives, scientists, Indigenous Peoples and youth—could participate under UNFCCC procedures. Official negotiating meetings were held in the registered-participant Blue Zone; the host-managed Green Zone was intended for public-facing activities.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the conference’s opening and its reported collapse over fossil-fuel language; it does not attempt to catalogue every negotiation text, side event, national statement or issue discussed during COP31.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this capture matter in Guasave?
explore_lenses.title: It targets a long-standing Sinaloa network
explore_lenses.summary: The arrest removes the alleged leader of an organization rooted in Guasave and tied to major U.S.-bound drug-trafficking allegations. It also occurred amid conflict among criminal factions in Sinaloa, making the immediate disruption to civilian safety especially consequential.

claims.text: The U.S. Treasury said in 2013 that the Meza Flores organization operated from Guasave and had distributed methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana and cocaine to the United States since 2000.

The FBI described Meza-Flores as the alleged leader of a heavily armed, Sinaloa-based trafficking organization, and said it was allegedly responsible for trafficking heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana.
The DEA characterized the capture as a significant blow to the organization, while Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch called it an important step toward pacifying Sinaloa.

explore_lenses.label: How did the situation reach this point?
explore_lenses.title: A long-running pursuit met a volatile local conflict
explore_lenses.summary: Mexican authorities arrested Meza-Flores after years of U.S. criminal cases and sanctions against his alleged organization. The operation came after recent security actions against his network and triggered an armed response in its home region.

claims.text: The FBI added Meza-Flores to its Ten Most Wanted list on February 4, 2025; it said he had been indicted in the District of Columbia in 2012 and faced a 2019 superseding indictment alleging drug-trafficking and firearms offenses.

The Justice Department says its 2019 indictment alleged that Meza-Flores conspired from 2005 through 2019 to import cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and marijuana into the United States; the department stresses that an indictment is an allegation and does not establish guilt.

Mexico’s Security Ministry said on October 28 that naval personnel, the ministry and federal prosecutors had acted against an alleged second-in-command of Meza-Flores’s group after an attack on naval personnel in Sinaloa; it said forensic confirmation of one identity was still pending.

According to reporting based on the Mexican military’s account, the November 20 operation used elite Army and National Guard units and also detained an alleged second-in-command and an alleged financial operator; the military later reported four service members and seven suspected attackers killed.

explore_lenses.summary: Authorities say security forces will remain in Sinaloa while prosecutors handle the detainee. Analysts warn that removing senior figures without dismantling their networks can prompt competition and further violence, but that is a forecast rather than an established outcome.

claims.text: Mexican authorities said Meza-Flores was flown to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors, and García Harfuch said armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa to protect civilians.
U.S. Justice Department material published before the arrest listed pending federal drug-trafficking cases against Meza-Flores in the Southern District of California and the District of Columbia.

The immediate backlash included gunfire, burning vehicles and roadblocks; AP reported that a federal official described at least 10 burning-vehicle roadblocks during the effort to move Meza-Flores out of Guasave.

story_report.summary: Mexican authorities captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” in Sinaloa, removing a man who had been on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list. The arrest was followed by violence in the region, including gunfire, burning vehicles and roadblocks. A federal official told AP that at least 10 burning-vehicle barricades were reported as authorities moved Meza-Flores out of Guasave, while security forces remained deployed to protect civilians.

sections.heading: Meza-Flores Organization and U.S. Cases
sections.body: U.S. Treasury said in 2013 that the Meza Flores organization operated from Guasave and had distributed methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana and cocaine to the United States since 2000. The FBI described Meza-Flores as the alleged leader of a heavily armed Sinaloa-based trafficking organization allegedly involved in heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana trafficking. The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted list in February 2025; Justice Department indictments alleged drug-trafficking and firearms offenses, allegations that do not establish guilt.

sections.heading: November Operation and Reported Casualties
sections.body: According to reporting based on the Mexican military’s account, the November 20 operation involved elite Army and National Guard units and also resulted in the detention of an alleged second-in-command and an alleged financial operator. The military later reported that four service members and seven suspected attackers were killed. Mexico’s Security Ministry had said in October that naval personnel, the ministry and federal prosecutors acted against an alleged second-in-command after an attack on naval personnel in Sinaloa, with forensic confirmation of one identity still pending.

sections.heading: Meza-Flores Custody and Sinaloa Security
sections.body: Mexican authorities said Meza-Flores was flown to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors, and Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch said armed forces would stay in Sinaloa to protect civilians. The DEA characterized the capture as a significant blow to the organization, while García Harfuch called it an important step toward pacifying the state. Separately, security analyst David Saucedo said the removal of the organization’s top two figures could fuel further violence because its broader armed, street-level and business networks remained.

unresolved.text: Public accounts have not fully explained how authorities located Meza-Flores or the specific scope of any U.S. intelligence assistance.
It remains unclear whether Mexico will prosecute Meza-Flores first, whether and when the United States will seek extradition, and who will take operational control of his network.
The arrest alone does not establish the organization’s remaining trafficking capacity or territorial control.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

explore_lenses.summary: The reported attack was a sequence rather than a single impact: local officials said ballistic missiles hit a busy central residential area, then drones struck as emergency crews worked. The casualty total rose through the following morning as more people sought treatment.

claims.text: Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the city administration, said two people—a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman—were killed; reporting put the wounded total at 60, including six children.

Local officials said the initial missiles struck a restaurant parking area in a densely populated part of the city, and subsequent drone strikes hit while medics, rescuers and utility workers were responding.
About 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and businesses were reported damaged; 28 injured people remained hospitalized in early updates.

story_report.summary: A Russian missile and drone attack on Kryvyi Rih, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown, killed two people and wounded 60, according to later reports. City administration head Oleksandr Vilkul identified those killed as a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman; six children were among the injured. The strikes hit a densely populated area, damaging homes, public facilities and businesses.

sections.heading: Damage and hospitalizations in Kryvyi Rih
sections.body: Local officials said the initial missiles hit a restaurant parking area in a densely populated part of the city. About 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and businesses were reported damaged. Early updates said 28 injured people remained in hospital.

sections.heading: Rescue workers struck during response
sections.body: Officials said further missiles and drones struck after medics, rescuers and utility workers had arrived at the scene. Local reporting said ambulance personnel and State Emergency Service workers were among those injured. Zelenskyy said no military facilities were near the impact area and characterized the attack as targeting civilians; the consulted reports did not provide a Russian public explanation or target justification for the strike.

sections.heading: War diplomacy remains unresolved
sections.body: The attack occurred as diplomatic questions over ending the Russia-Ukraine war remained unsettled. Al Jazeera reported that U.S. President Donald Trump said Vladimir Putin wanted a diplomatic end to the war, while Zelenskyy said he was less convinced Russia was ready to compromise. Moscow was reported to be demanding Ukraine’s withdrawal from the entire Donbas region, which Kyiv rejects, while security-guarantee discussions remained unresolved.

unresolved.text: The reported injury total changed from 58 in earlier official updates to 60 in later reporting, and the available accounts do not provide a final independently audited casualty count.
The consulted reporting did not establish a timetable for further talks or an agreement on territory or security guarantees.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

explore_lenses.label: What was hit and how large was the barrage?
explore_lenses.title: A nationwide strike with Kyiv infrastructure targets
explore_lenses.summary: The Kyiv damage was part of a wider overnight Russian drone-and-missile attack rather than an isolated strike on the capital. Ukrainian military reporting recorded impacts across multiple locations, while footage and reporting from Kyiv showed damage to housing, offices, warehouses, hospitals, utilities and bridges.

claims.text: Ukraine’s General Staff said Russia launched 404 attack drones, 84 cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and Zircon missiles from the evening of November 19 into November 20; it reported 23 impact locations and debris falls at 10 others.

Euronews, citing Ukrainian authorities and emergency services, reported that strikes damaged residential and commercial buildings, hospitals, essential infrastructure and three bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy characterized the targets as civilian life-supporting infrastructure, including energy facilities, logistics and bridges; this is Ukraine’s assessment of the strike’s targeting.

story_report.summary: Russia’s overnight assault on November 20 killed at least eight people across Ukraine, including six in Kyiv, according to Euronews, while President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said authorities knew of eight deaths and nearly 30 injuries. Strikes damaged buildings and warehouses in the capital, where emergency crews searched wreckage, fought fires and began restoring services. The differing injury figures reflected an unfolding rescue operation and preliminary casualty accounting.

sections.heading: Scale of the Russian Assault
sections.body: Ukraine’s General Staff said Russia launched 404 attack drones and 84 cruise, ballistic and Zircon missiles from the evening of November 19 into November 20. It reported 23 impact locations and debris falls at 10 others. Zelenskyy said the targets included civilian life-supporting infrastructure such as energy facilities, logistics and bridges, an assessment that does not independently establish the intended target of every weapon.

sections.heading: Damage and Rescue Work in Kyiv
sections.body: Euronews reported damage to residential and commercial buildings, hospitals, essential infrastructure and three bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv. Responders continued searching damaged structures, extinguishing remaining fires, clearing rubble, documenting evidence and restoring essential services after some blazes were brought under control. Zelenskyy said restoration work had begun where security conditions permitted and that repair deadlines had been set.

sections.heading: Ukraine Seeks Air-Defense Support
sections.body: Zelenskyy said he had instructed the Foreign Ministry to contact partners preparing air-defense packages and that Ukrainian officials were discussing PAC-2 and PAC-3 missile supplies with U.S. counterparts. The request did not confirm a new delivery. Ukraine’s General Staff also reported that Russia launched a further three ballistic missiles and 148 drones overnight into November 21, indicating the immediate aerial threat had continued.

unresolved.text: No final, independently verified casualty total or definitive count limited specifically to Kyiv was available while rescue operations continued.
The available Ukrainian strike totals were preliminary, and the intended target of each weapon has not been independently established.
The sources do not confirm whether or when additional air-defense interceptors will be delivered, or the full timetable for repairs.

stories.title: Man Convicted of Arson for 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
stories.summary: A federal jury has convicted a 30-year-old man of arson for starting the 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles, which resulted in 12 fatalities and the destruction of over 6,800 buildings. This conviction follows a retrial after the initial case ended in a mistrial earlier this year. Prosecutors indicated that the defendant had been experiencing significant personal distress leading up to the fire.

explore_lenses.label: Why does the conviction matter beyond one defendant?
explore_lenses.title: It establishes criminal responsibility, not every cause of loss
explore_lenses.summary: The verdict holds Jonathan Rinderknecht criminally liable for starting the fire that prosecutors said later rekindled into the Palisades Fire. It does not resolve separate civil allegations about whether agencies' suppression, inspection, or water-supply decisions worsened the disaster.

claims.text: A federal jury convicted Rinderknecht of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce; the Justice Department said the January 2025 fire killed 12 people, destroyed 6,837 structures, and caused an estimated $25 billion in damage.

In civil litigation, fire victims have alleged that public agencies failed to adequately inspect the Lachman Fire burn area or maintain adequate water resources; these are allegations in a lawsuit, not findings made by the criminal jury.

explore_lenses.label: Why would an NCIC breach matter nationally?
explore_lenses.title: A shared operational system is at issue
explore_lenses.summary: NCIC is not a single-agency archive: it is the FBI-operated system through which authorized agencies across the country exchange time-sensitive criminal-justice records. Its importance lies in both the sensitivity of the data and officers’ reliance on timely, accurate search results.

claims.text: The FBI's privacy assessment says NCIC links criminal and authorized noncriminal justice agencies in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, U.S. territories, select foreign countries, and operates around the clock.

Authorized users query NCIC for functions including fugitive apprehension, missing-person cases, stolen-property recovery, protection orders, sex-offender monitoring, and firearms- and weapons-related background checks.

NCIC's records are supplied by participating agencies, which are responsible for their accuracy, timeliness, and completeness; that shared structure means any confirmed integrity problem could require coordination beyond the FBI.

stories.title: International Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has made a historic ruling, declaring Myanmar guilty of genocide against the Rohingya minority during a military campaign in 2017. This unprecedented decision, which found intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population, marks the first time a state has been held accountable for genocide by the ICJ. The ruling has sparked varied international reactions, with Myanmar rejecting it as 'unfair' and calls for sanctions against the country emerging from rights groups. The ICJ's decision may also influence future cases regarding genocide, including allegations against Israel.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a genocide finding?
explore_lenses.title: A seven-year state-to-state case
explore_lenses.summary: The judgment followed proceedings begun by The Gambia in 2019 over Myanmar's obligations under the Genocide Convention, rather than a criminal trial of individual commanders. Public merits hearings in January 2026 drew on survivor, expert, documentary and geospatial evidence assembled in part by a UN investigative mechanism.

claims.text: The Gambia instituted the case in November 2019, alleging Genocide Convention violations against Rohingya during Myanmar military operations in 2016 and 2017; the ICJ heard merits arguments and testimony in January 2026.

The UN's Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar says it supplied the parties with nine analytical reports, 40 witness statements, material from military defectors, geospatial analysis and other evidence; both parties cited its work at the hearings.

Myanmar's Foreign Ministry had argued before the judgment that The Gambia's allegations were flawed and based on biased and unreliable reports, while saying it would defend its case within the legal framework of the Genocide Convention.

explore_lenses.label: What is Myanmar now required to do?
explore_lenses.title: Binding duties, but limited enforcement
explore_lenses.summary: The UN says the final, non-appealable judgment requires Myanmar to stop any continuing Convention violations, investigate and punish perpetrators, prevent recurrence and provide reparations. Implementation depends principally on Myanmar, while the Court has no direct enforcement arm.

claims.text: According to the UN Secretary-General's statement, the Court found Myanmar responsible for killing Rohingya, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births during the 2017 operations, with intent to destroy a substantial part of the group.

The UN says Myanmar must take steps including investigations, prosecutions where appropriate, legal measures, guarantees of non-repetition, and adequate and prompt reparations, including safe, voluntary and dignified return and family reunification.
The ruling is legally binding and final, but the ICJ cannot directly compel compliance; noncompliance can be taken to the UN Security Council.

Myanmar's government said before the ruling that it was committed to repatriation through arrangements with Bangladesh and UN agencies, conditioned on circumstances permitting safe, voluntary and dignified returns.

sections.heading: The Gambia’s Genocide Case
sections.body: The Gambia brought the case in November 2019, alleging that Myanmar violated the Genocide Convention during military operations in 2016 and 2017. The ICJ heard arguments and testimony on the merits in January 2026. The UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar provided the parties with analytical reports, witness statements, material from military defectors and geospatial analysis; both sides cited its work during the hearings.

sections.body: Before the judgment, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said The Gambia’s case relied on biased and unreliable reports and that it would contest the allegations within the Genocide Convention’s legal framework. sections.heading: Rohingya Return and Compliance
sections.body: According to the UN secretary-general, Myanmar must pursue investigations and prosecutions where appropriate, legal measures, guarantees of non-repetition, and prompt, adequate reparations. Compliance also includes safe, voluntary and dignified return for those who fled, including family reunification. The court cannot directly compel compliance, though noncompliance can be referred to the UN Security Council; the judgment may also provide a precedent for future genocide cases.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

event_overview.title: About Gaza Conflict
event_overview.subject: Gaza Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Gaza Conflict refers here to the war and continuing violence involving Israel, Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups that followed the 7 October 2023 attacks from Gaza into Israel and Israel’s subsequent military campaign in the Gaza Strip. A ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025 and ended large-scale hostilities, but United Nations reporting as of 21 November 2026 described continued Israeli strikes, shooting and shelling, Palestinian casualties, access restrictions and severe humanitarian needs in Gaza.

facts.label: Start and current status
facts.value: The present war began on 7 October 2023, when Palestinian armed groups from Gaza attacked communities and military sites in southern Israel and Israel began strikes on Gaza. A ceasefire effective 10 October 2025 ended large-scale hostilities but did not end violence.

facts.label: Location and principal parties
facts.value: The core theatre is the Gaza Strip and nearby areas of Israel. The conflict involves Israeli forces and Hamas alongside other Palestinian armed groups; civilians in Gaza and Israel have been directly affected.

facts.label: Pre-war context
facts.value: The United Nations describes Gaza as having been under an Israeli blockade of varying intensity since 2007, with recurrent escalations between Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups before the 2023 war.

facts.label: Humanitarian and diplomatic framework
facts.value: UN Security Council Resolution 2728, adopted on 25 March 2024, demanded a Ramadan ceasefire leading to a lasting sustainable ceasefire, release of hostages, humanitarian access and compliance with international law. The 2025 ceasefire was supported by mediation involving Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye and the United States.

facts.label: International legal proceedings
facts.value: South Africa instituted proceedings against Israel at the International Court of Justice on 29 December 2023 under the Genocide Convention. The Court has issued provisional-measures orders; these are interim directions and do not decide the case’s final merits.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows particular Gaza-related military, diplomatic and accountability developments from August to September 2026; it does not provide a complete record of the war, ceasefire implementation, humanitarian response, legal proceedings or events affecting Israel and the wider region.

stories.title: Morocco Invests €366 Million in National Defence Industry Development by 2035
stories.summary: Morocco has announced a commitment of €366 million to establish a national defence industry by 2035. The plan aims to fulfill 40% of the armed forces' and security services' equipment needs through domestic production and to generate over 65% of industry revenues from exports. This initiative will be supported by a new strategic agency, a holding company, and the development of two new industrial zones.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

event_overview.title: About Ukraine War
event_overview.subject: Ukraine War
event_overview.summary: The Ukraine War is the interstate conflict centered on Russia’s use of armed force against Ukraine, with roots in Russia’s 2014 seizure of Crimea and fighting in eastern Ukraine and a full-scale Russian invasion launched on February 24, 2022. It combines active military operations, diplomacy over a possible settlement, international assistance and sanctions, displacement, and investigations into alleged international crimes.

facts.label: Conflict timeline
facts.value: The broader conflict dates to 2014; the International Court of Justice’s March 16, 2022 order identifies the Russian military operations at issue as having commenced in Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

facts.label: Parties and geography
facts.value: The war principally concerns Ukraine and the Russian Federation and is fought on Ukrainian territory; Belarus has also been cited by the European Union for involvement in Russia’s 2022 invasion.

facts.label: International legal framework
facts.value: The UN Charter requires members to refrain from the threat or use of force against another state’s territorial integrity or political independence. The UN General Assembly adopted resolution ES-11/1 on March 2, 2022, titled “Aggression against Ukraine,” by a vote of 141–5 with 35 abstentions.

facts.label: International court proceedings
facts.value: In provisional measures issued March 16, 2022, the ICJ ordered Russia to suspend the military operations it had commenced on February 24, 2022; the order was made in Ukraine’s case under the Genocide Convention and did not resolve the merits of the dispute.

facts.label: Accountability process
facts.value: The International Criminal Court opened its Ukraine investigation on March 2, 2022. Its stated scope covers alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, or genocide committed by any person on any part of Ukraine’s territory since November 21, 2013.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows selected diplomacy and security developments connected to the war, including proposed leader-level contacts and regional military incidents; it does not aim to provide a complete record of battlefield operations, negotiations, sanctions, humanitarian impacts, or legal proceedings.

event_overview.title: About US-Russia Relations
event_overview.subject: US-Russia Relations
event_overview.summary: U.S.-Russia relations encompass diplomatic, security, economic and arms-control issues between two nuclear-armed permanent members of the UN Security Council. The Shenzhen meetings place a U.S.-Russia leader-level engagement within China’s 2026 APEC host year, alongside a separate three-leader discussion involving China.

facts.label: Diplomatic relations
facts.value: The United States recognized the Russian Federation as the Soviet Union’s successor on December 25, 1991, and established diplomatic relations with it on December 31, 1991.

facts.label: Meeting setting
facts.value: China hosted APEC in 2026, and Shenzhen hosted the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting on November 19, 2026; APEC describes itself as a forum of 21 member economies.

facts.label: Format and participants
facts.value: The talks included a separate Trump-Putin meeting and a subsequent face-to-face meeting among U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the margins of the Shenzhen APEC gathering.

facts.label: Arms-control context
facts.value: New START, the bilateral treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic offensive arms, entered into force on February 5, 2011 and was extended through February 4, 2026; its expiration makes nuclear-risk and arms-control issues a central context for later leader-level discussions.

facts.label: Economic and legal context
facts.value: U.S. Russia-related sanctions operate through multiple executive and statutory authorities, including Ukraine-/Russia-related measures, Russian Harmful Foreign Activities sanctions and CAATSA; the scope of restrictions and licenses varies by program.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the November 18-19, 2026 leader meetings in China, not the full history of U.S.-Russia diplomacy, sanctions, the war in Ukraine, or all APEC proceedings.

explore_lenses.label: What did the trilateral declaration actually do?
explore_lenses.title: A narrow statement on four shared areas
explore_lenses.summary: The November 19 declaration confirmed a new three-way channel but set out broad commitments rather than operational agreements on the conflicts and disputes surrounding the summit.

claims.text: The joint declaration commits the United States, China and Russia to pursue U.N. reform, support stable refined-petroleum supplies, oppose what it calls jurisdictional abuse by the International Criminal Court, and hold a dialogue on nuclear-risk reduction and nonproliferation.
The declaration does not mention the Ukraine war, Taiwan, or artificial intelligence; it therefore does not document a trilateral settlement, enforcement mechanism, or timetable on those issues.

Xi characterized the summit as a step toward managing major-power differences through mutual respect, dialogue and cooperation; that is China's stated framing, not evidence that the underlying disputes were resolved.

explore_lenses.title: Existing trade channel remains the clearest mechanism
explore_lenses.summary: Before the summit, Washington and Beijing had already created a Board of Trade process for potential reciprocal tariff reductions. The summit did not publicly announce a completed trade package.

Bessent said the Shenzhen bilateral included a "robust discussion" of trade but identified no specific agreement, and Reuters reported that administration officials had said no Board of Trade agreements would be announced on the trip.

story_report.summary: After a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump said his relationships with both leaders were “fantastic” and announced an agreement with Xi on artificial-intelligence guardrails. The meetings produced limited publicly detailed results, however, leaving key issues without a documented resolution. A joint declaration set out areas for further cooperation but did not address Taiwan, the Ukraine war or AI, while trade discussions yielded no announced agreement.

sections.heading: Trilateral Declaration Sets Limited Agenda
sections.body: The U.S.-Russia-China declaration commits the three governments to pursue U.N. reform, support stable refined-petroleum supplies, oppose what it calls International Criminal Court jurisdictional abuse, and hold dialogue on nuclear-risk reduction and nonproliferation. It contains no reference to the Ukraine war, Taiwan or artificial intelligence, and provides no documented settlement, enforcement mechanism or timetable on those subjects. Xi described the summit as an effort to manage major-power differences through mutual respect, dialogue and cooperation.

sections.heading: Military AI Guardrails Remain Undefined
sections.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Trump and Xi agreed that humans should remain involved in military decisions using AI and that major military operations should not be launched without human involvement. But the trilateral declaration does not include AI, leaving the reported U.S.-China understanding without a stated legal status, scope, verification process or stated applicability. Bessent also said the arrangement would coexist with competition for technological leadership and described U.S. policy as de-risking rather than economic decoupling.

sections.heading: Trade Decisions Remain for Later Talks
sections.body: A pre-existing U.S.-China Board of Trade is tasked with considering reciprocal reduced-tariff treatment for mutually agreed import lists totaling roughly $30 billion on each side, with Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng named as principals. Bessent described a robust trade discussion but identified no agreement, and Reuters reported that officials had said no Board of Trade deals would be announced during the trip. Reuters said final tariff decisions appeared likely to be deferred to a possible mid-December G20 meeting in Miami.

unresolved.text: The declaration sets no implementation arrangements, responsible agencies, deadlines or follow-up meeting date.
No jointly issued text specifies which AI systems or decisions the reported guardrails cover, or how compliance would be assessed.
Public materials do not confirm a Miami meeting, the goods that could receive tariff changes, or whether either side will extend the tariff truce.

explore_lenses.label: Why was the 2027 closure deadline pushed back?
explore_lenses.title: Construction and population pressures drove the reset
explore_lenses.summary: The 2032 target replaces a legally mandated August 2027 closure date that the administration says it cannot meet. The revised schedule ties final closure to completion of the four borough facilities and the reduction of the daily jail population.

claims.text: New York City is legally required to stop using Rikers for incarceration by August 2027; the mayor's proposal would require City Council approval to move that deadline.

The Board of Correction reported an average daily jail population of 6,747 from January through May 2026, while the administration's plan is designed around a 4,100-person system after full implementation.

The administration attributes the recent population increase chiefly to longer stays in custody, citing pandemic-era court delays and other system factors; this is the city's explanation, not an independent causal finding in the plan.
